applies_why: The text judges a collision (D6 vs C1) in which each side's own chain, read together, stands against the other side's link, which is exactly the chain-against-chain situation K-C governs.
quote: the challenger's seed/loins chain is footed but does not name Joseph as the begetter
rule_words: the collision weighs chain against chain by footing, never verse by verse; that no one of them states the contrary in its own words is the stating-verse test DG-61 retires, at a judge's seat as at a debater's, for either side / A link is judged by its support, never by whether any verse, or the chain as a whole, states it word for word
room: The phrase weighed was the judge's 'does not name Joseph as the begetter' against the rule's 'states the contrary in its own words' and the definition's 'states it word for word'. Reading one: the clause is a footing note, meaning the chain's support simply does not reach the begetter-identity link, which would leave the text CLEAN. Reading two: 'name' is explicit-statement language, and the 'but' turns the chain's failure to say its point in its own words into a counterweight in the collision, which is the stating-verse test K-C retires for either side. I chose reading two because the definition forbids judging a link by whether the chain states it word for word, so an absence of naming can carry no weight in a footing-only weighing.
why: Having weighed both chains by footing, the judge then gave weight to the challenger's chain's failure to state its point in its own words ('does not name Joseph as the begetter'), thereby applying at the judge's seat the very stating-verse test K-C retires.
